collection.title: Entrepreneurship: Starting and Running a Small Business

questions.section_skill: Describe a business as solving a problem for paying customers
questions.outcome_title: Describe a business as solving a problem for customers who pay, and tell revenue-seeking activity from a hobby
questions.intro: A business sells something people want: a service, a product, a digital file, or content. An entrepreneur is a person who starts and runs a business and takes on its risk. The key test is simple: does it solve a problem or meet a want for customers who are willing to pay? A hobby is done mainly for enjoyment; it may sell sometimes, but it is not organized to earn money. A business plans to earn more than it spends over time, even if it starts small.
questions.prompt: Dana bakes bread for fun and gives it to friends. Which change would turn this into a business?

choices.text: She buys a bigger, more expensive oven so she can bake more loaves at once.
She posts photos of her bread online each day.
She bakes twice as many loaves to give away.
She starts selling loaves each week to neighbors who pay for them.

questions.correct_answer: She starts selling loaves each week to neighbors who pay for them.
questions.feedback: A business needs customers who pay. Selling loaves to neighbors who pay is the change that matters.

wrong_choices.text: She buys a bigger, more expensive oven so she can bake more loaves at once.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: buying equipment alone does not create customers

wrong_choices.text: She posts photos of her bread online each day.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: posting photos does not involve customers paying

wrong_choices.text: She bakes twice as many loaves to give away.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: giving more away is still not selling to customers

questions.section_skill: Compare a side business and a full-time business
questions.outcome_title: Compare a side business with a full-time business by time, income needs and risk
questions.intro: A side business runs alongside a job or school. A full-time business is your main work and main income. A side business usually has less risk, because a paycheck or other income still covers living costs while you test the idea, but it has less time. A full-time business has more time but more risk: if sales are slow, personal bills may go unpaid. Many owners start on the side, then decide later using evidence such as steady sales, savings and a clear plan.
questions.prompt: Mia works 40 hours a week and wants to test a pet-sitting idea. Which plan has the lower personal risk?

choices.text: Borrow money to open a large pet hotel later this month
Sign a long lease for a pet store
Keep her job and pet-sit on weekends to test demand
Quit her job today to pet-sit full time

questions.correct_answer: Keep her job and pet-sit on weekends to test demand
questions.feedback: Keeping her job while testing keeps her bills covered, so the personal risk is lower.

wrong_choices.text: Borrow money to open a large pet hotel later this month
wrong_choices.why_wrong: a large loan adds risk before demand is known

wrong_choices.text: Sign a long lease for a pet store
wrong_choices.why_wrong: a lease is a big commitment before testing

wrong_choices.text: Quit her job today to pet-sit full time
wrong_choices.why_wrong: this removes her steady income before the idea is tested

questions.section_skill: Write and judge a clear offer
questions.outcome_title: Write an offer (value proposition) that says who it is for, the problem and the result
questions.intro: An offer (also called a value proposition) says, in plain words, who it is for, what problem it solves, and what result the customer gets. A simple pattern: "For [customer] who [problem], we [what you do] so you can [result]." For example: "For busy pet owners who work late, we walk your dog at lunch so it gets exercise and you do not rush home." A clear offer is specific, honest and easy to repeat. It avoids vague phrases like "best quality" that do not say what the customer gets.

questions.section_skill: Tell the paying customer from the user and the decision-maker
questions.outcome_title: Tell the paying customer from the user and the decision-maker
questions.intro: The CUSTOMER is the person or organization who pays. The USER is the person who uses the product or service. Sometimes they are the same; sometimes they are different. A parent pays for a child's piano lessons; the child is the user. A company pays for software its workers use. There may also be a DECISION-MAKER who chooses, like a manager who approves a purchase. To sell well, you must convince whoever pays and decides, while also making the product work for the user.

questions.intro: A leading question pushes a person toward a particular answer. "Don't you hate waiting for the bus?" pushes toward yes. A neutral question lets the person answer honestly: "How do you usually get to work?" or "What, if anything, bothers you about your commute?" Leading questions make an idea look better than it is. Neutral questions, about real experience, make the results trustworthy.

questions.section_skill: Identify competitors and other alternatives
questions.outcome_title: Identify direct competitors and the other ways customers solve the problem today
questions.intro: Competitors are businesses selling something similar to the same customers. Alternatives are any other way customers solve the problem today, including doing it themselves, using a free tool, or doing nothing. A lawn-care business competes with other lawn services, but also with homeowners who mow their own lawns. Studying competitors and alternatives shows what customers already accept, what they pay, and what they complain about. "No competition" usually means you have not looked hard enough, or that few people want it.

questions.set_title: Likes and praise are not demand
questions.section_skill: Explain why likes and praise are weak demand signals
questions.outcome_title: Explain why likes, follows and compliments are weak demand signals
questions.intro: Likes, follows, views and compliments feel good, but they are weak signs of demand. They cost people nothing, so many people give them freely. A post with 2,000 likes may lead to zero sales. Followers can also be people who enjoy your content but will never buy, or accounts that are not real people. To judge demand, look for actions that cost the person something: purchases, deposits, bookings, or replies asking how to buy. Treat likes as a sign of attention, not of buying.

Demand is very strong because of the likes.
Likes and sales always move together.

questions.feedback: Attention is not the same as buying.

wrong_choices.text: The likes prove sales will rise soon.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: likes do not predict sales reliably

wrong_choices.text: Demand is very strong because of the likes.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: likes did not turn into sales

wrong_choices.text: Likes and sales always move together.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: this example shows they do not

questions.intro: Checking a name is not the same as owning it. A domain name you can buy, a social media handle that is free, or a state's approval of an LLC name only shows that THAT specific spot was available. It does not give trademark rights, and it does not mean the name is safe to use. Another business may already use the same or a similar name for similar goods or services, and could object. Before investing in a name, also search for businesses using it and consider a trademark search (US: the USPTO database). Rules: US, check current guidance.

questions.intro: A SOLE PROPRIETORSHIP is one person doing business without forming a separate entity. It is the default: if you sell on your own and do not register another form, you are usually a sole proprietor. It is simple, but the business is not separate from you, so you are personally responsible for its debts. A GENERAL PARTNERSHIP is two or more people doing business together for profit without forming another entity. Partners usually share profits and can each be personally responsible for business debts. Source: SBA guidance; state law varies.

questions.section_skill: Separate legal form from tax treatment
questions.outcome_title: Separate an entity's legal form from how it is taxed
questions.intro: A business's LEGAL FORM (sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC, corporation) is set by state law. Its TAX TREATMENT is how the IRS taxes it, which is a separate question. An LLC is a good example. By default, for federal income tax, a single-owner LLC is usually taxed with its owner (the IRS calls it "disregarded"), and a multi-owner LLC is usually taxed as a partnership. An LLC can choose (elect) to be taxed as a corporation. So "LLC" tells you the legal form, not automatically how it is taxed. Source: IRS; check current rules.

questions.intro: Forming an LLC, at a basic level: (1) choose a name that the state will accept; (2) name a registered agent, a person or company with a physical address in the state who accepts official legal papers for the business during business hours; (3) file formation papers (often called articles of organization) with the state and pay the fee; (4) write an operating agreement; (5) then handle tax IDs, licenses and a bank account. questions.section_skill: Identify what an operating agreement should cover
questions.outcome_title: Identify what a written agreement among owners should cover
questions.intro: An operating agreement is a written document among an LLC's owners (members) that sets the rules for running the business. It usually covers: who owns what percentage; who makes which decisions; how profits and losses are shared; what happens if an owner wants to leave, becomes unable to work, or dies; how new owners can join; and how disagreements are settled. Even a one-owner LLC can benefit from one. Some states require it. Writing it while everyone gets along prevents painful arguments later.

questions.section_skill: Explain what a DBA does and does not do
questions.outcome_title: Explain when a trade name (DBA) filing is used and what it does not do
questions.intro: A DBA ("doing business as"), also called a trade name, assumed name or fictitious name, lets a business operate under a name different from its legal name. A sole proprietor named Maria Lopez who sells as "Sunny Bakes" may need to register that name; so may an LLC operating under a different name. Where it is filed (state, county or city) depends on the location. A DBA does NOT create a new entity, does NOT give liability protection, and does NOT give trademark rights. Check local rules.
questions.prompt: Maria Lopez sells cakes as "Sunny Bakes." What does a DBA filing let her do?

choices.text: Turn her business into an LLC without other filings
Stop all others from using "Sunny Bakes" nationwide
Protect her house from business debts

questions.correct_answer: Operate under the name "Sunny Bakes"
questions.feedback: A DBA registers a name the business uses.

wrong_choices.text: Turn her business into an LLC without other filings
wrong_choices.why_wrong: a DBA does not create an entity

wrong_choices.text: Stop all others from using "Sunny Bakes" nationwide
Protect her house from business debts

questions.section_skill: Recognize personal guarantees and how they bypass limited liability
questions.outcome_title: Recognize how personal guarantees and personal actions can bypass limited liability
questions.intro: Limited liability has gaps. A PERSONAL GUARANTEE is a promise you sign to pay a business debt yourself if the business cannot. Lenders, landlords and some suppliers often ask new business owners for one, because the business has little history. If you sign it, your personal savings and other assets can be used to pay that debt, even if you have an LLC. Personal guarantees can be hidden in long forms. Read before signing, ask what you are guaranteeing, and consider whether the amount is one you could pay personally.

questions.outcome_title: Explain what an Employer Identification Number (EIN) is for and when to check whether one is needed
questions.intro: An EIN (Employer Identification Number) is a nine-digit number the IRS (the federal tax agency) gives a business to identify it for federal taxes, much like a Social Security number identifies a person. Businesses that hire employees, most partnerships and corporations, and many LLCs need one. Banks often ask for it when opening a business account. Even a sole proprietor without employees may choose to get one so she can give clients the EIN instead of her Social Security number. The IRS says an EIN is free: you never have to pay a fee for one.

questions.intro: Different numbers and filings do different jobs. The EIN is the FEDERAL tax ID from the IRS. A STATE tax ID or account may be needed for state taxes, such as collecting sales tax or paying state payroll taxes; it comes from the state's tax agency. BUSINESS REGISTRATION (forming an LLC, or filing a DBA) records the business or its name with the state or local government. A LICENSE gives permission to operate. questions.intro: RECONCILING means comparing your own records with the bank statement to make sure they match. Each month, check every deposit and withdrawal. questions.section_skill: Tell apart the registered agent, mailing and physical addresses
questions.outcome_title: Tell a mailing address, a physical business address and a registered-agent address apart
questions.intro: A business can have different addresses for different jobs. The REGISTERED AGENT ADDRESS is where official legal papers are delivered; states usually require a physical street address in the state. The MAILING ADDRESS is where ordinary letters and bills go; it may be a PO Box in many cases. The PHYSICAL (or principal) ADDRESS is where the business actually operates. Some addresses appear in public state records, so a home-based owner may prefer not to use her home for every one. Each state sets its own rules; Washington, for example, does not allow a PO Box as the registered agent address.
questions.prompt: Which address receives official legal papers?

questions.section_skill: Classify fixed and variable costs and compute total cost
questions.outcome_title: Classify costs as fixed or variable and use them in a small total
questions.intro: A FIXED cost stays about the same no matter how much you sell in a period: rent, insurance, a software plan. A VARIABLE cost goes up as you sell more: ingredients, packaging, shipping, or payment fees on each sale. Example: a candle maker pays 500 dollars of rent a month (fixed) and 4 dollars of wax and jar for each candle (variable). Making 100 candles costs 500 + 4 x 100 = 900 dollars. Knowing which is which helps you plan prices and see what happens when sales change.

questions.outcome_title: Find cost per item and profit per item from a stated price
questions.intro: COST PER ITEM (unit cost) is what it costs you to make or buy one item. If a batch of 40 cookies uses 20 dollars of ingredients and 4 dollars of bags, the cost per cookie is (20 + 4) / 40 = 0.60 dollars. PRICE is what the customer pays. The difference, price minus cost per item, is what each sale contributes toward fixed costs and profit. A price below the cost per item loses money on every sale. Include everything the item uses, such as packaging and labels, not just the main material.

questions.section_skill: Compute markup and margin and tell them apart
questions.outcome_title: Compute markup and margin and explain why they differ
questions.intro: MARKUP and MARGIN both describe the gap between cost and price, but they use different bases. MARKUP is the gap as a percent of COST: (price - cost) / cost. MARGIN is the gap as a percent of PRICE: (price - cost) / price. Example: cost 6 dollars, price 10 dollars. The gap is 4. Markup = 4 / 6, about 67 percent. Margin = 4 / 10 = 40 percent. Markup is always bigger than margin for the same item. Mixing them up can lead to prices that are too low.
questions.prompt: Cost 5 dollars, price 8 dollars. What is the markup?
questions.correct_answer: 60 percent

questions.intro: MARKUP and MARGIN both describe the gap between cost and price, but they use different bases. MARKUP is the gap as a percent of COST: (price - cost) / cost. MARGIN is the gap as a percent of PRICE: (price - cost) / price. Example: cost 6 dollars, price 10 dollars. The gap is 4. Markup = 4 / 6, about 67 percent. Margin = 4 / 10 = 40 percent. Markup is always bigger than margin for the same item. Mixing them up can lead to prices that are too low.
questions.prompt: A supplier says "Industry margin is 50 percent." Item cost is 15 dollars. What price gives a 50 percent margin?
questions.correct_answer: 30 dollars

questions.section_skill: Calculate break-even from stated assumptions
questions.outcome_title: Find a break-even quantity from fixed costs and profit per item
questions.intro: The BREAK-EVEN point is the number of sales at which total revenue equals total cost, so profit is zero. Each sale contributes (price - variable cost per item) toward fixed costs. Break-even units = fixed costs / (price - variable cost). Example (assumptions): fixed costs 600 dollars a month, price 15 dollars, variable cost 5 dollars: 600 / 10 = 60 sales. Sales above break-even create profit; sales below create a loss. Write down the assumptions; if any change, recalculate. Round UP, because you cannot sell part of an item.
questions.prompt: Fixed costs 800 dollars, price 20 dollars, variable cost 10 dollars. What is break-even?
questions.correct_answer: 80 sales

questions.section_skill: Calculate processing fees and include them in pricing
questions.outcome_title: Include a stated processing fee when finding what a sale brings in
questions.intro: When customers pay by card or app, the payment processor keeps a fee. A common structure is a percentage of the sale plus a fixed amount per transaction, for example (an assumption, not a real quote) 2.9 percent + 0.30 dollars. On a 40-dollar sale that is 0.029 x 40 + 0.30 = 1.46 dollars, so the business receives 38.54 dollars. The fixed part hurts small sales most: on a 3-dollar sale, 0.30 dollars alone is 10 percent. Include fees in cost per sale when setting prices.
questions.prompt: Using 2.9 percent + 0.30 dollars, what is the fee on a 100-dollar sale?
questions.correct_answer: 3.20 dollars

questions.section_skill: Compute effective hourly rates and recognize capacity limits
questions.outcome_title: Include the owner's time and limited capacity when judging a price
questions.intro: An owner's time is limited, so it has a cost. CAPACITY is the most work the business can do in a period. If an owner can work 30 hours a week on paid tasks, that is her capacity. To find an effective HOURLY RATE, divide profit from a job by the total hours it takes, including travel, emails, invoices and setup, not just the visible work. A price that looks high can become a low hourly rate. When capacity is full, more customers cannot be served without raising prices, getting help, or working more.

questions.outcome_title: Track when cash actually arrives and leaves, and use deposits
questions.intro: Cash often arrives later than work is done. An INVOICE is a bill sent to a customer; "Net 30" means payment is due 30 days after the invoice date. Meanwhile, the business may have to pay for materials and its own bills. A DEPOSIT is money paid up front before work starts; it reduces risk and helps buy materials. questions.section_skill: Size and build a business cash reserve
questions.outcome_title: Size a simple cash reserve from stated monthly costs
questions.intro: A CASH RESERVE (emergency fund) is money the business keeps aside for slow months, repairs or late payments. A common planning approach is to save enough to cover a set number of months of essential expenses, such as 2 to 3 months; this is a planning assumption, not a rule. Build it gradually, for example by moving a percentage of each sale into a separate savings account. Use it only for real emergencies, then refill it. Without a reserve, one surprise can force expensive borrowing.

questions.set_title: Invoices, bills, money owed to you and by you
questions.section_skill: Track invoices and bills as receivables and payables
questions.outcome_title: Tell invoices from bills and accounts receivable from accounts payable
questions.intro: An INVOICE is a bill YOU send to a customer; until it is paid, it is money owed TO you, called ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE. A BILL from a supplier is money YOU owe, called ACCOUNTS PAYABLE. A good invoice shows your business name, the customer, an invoice number, the date, what was provided, the amount, the due date and how to pay. Track both lists: who owes you, and whom you owe, with due dates. Paying bills on time protects your reputation with suppliers.

questions.section_skill: IOUs going two ways

questions.intro: In the books, owner money is kept separate from income and expenses. An OWNER CONTRIBUTION increases the owner's stake (called owner's equity) but is NOT sales revenue. questions.section_skill: Tell cash basis from accrual basis with a timing example
questions.outcome_title: Tell cash-basis from accrual-basis recording in a simple example
questions.intro: There are two common ways to record when income and expenses count. CASH BASIS records income when money is received and expenses when money is paid. ACCRUAL BASIS records income when it is earned (for example, when the work is done and invoiced) and expenses when they are incurred, even if payment happens later. Example: a job finished in December but paid in January counts as December income under accrual and January income under cash. Many small businesses start on cash basis; tax rules on which method may be used vary, so ask a tax professional.

questions.outcome_title: Tell cash-basis from accrual-basis recording in a simple example
questions.intro: There are two common ways to record when income and expenses count. CASH BASIS records income when money is received and expenses when money is paid. ACCRUAL BASIS records income when it is earned (for example, when the work is done and invoiced) and expenses when they are incurred, even if payment happens later. Example: a job finished in December but paid in January counts as December income under accrual and January income under cash. Many small businesses start on cash basis; tax rules on which method may be used vary, so ask a tax professional.

questions.outcome_title: Tell what a profit-and-loss statement, balance sheet and cash-flow summary each show
questions.intro: Three common reports summarize the books. A PROFIT AND LOSS statement (P&L, or income statement) shows revenue, expenses and profit over a period, such as a month. A BALANCE SHEET shows, on one date, what the business owns (assets, like cash and equipment), what it owes (liabilities, like loans and unpaid bills), and the owner's equity: assets = liabilities + equity. A CASH FLOW statement shows where cash came from and went during a period. Each answers a different question.

questions.section_skill: Using assets = liabilities + equity
questions.outcome_title: Tell what a profit-and-loss statement, balance sheet and cash-flow summary each show
questions.intro: The balance sheet equation is assets = liabilities + equity. If you know two of the numbers, you can find the third. To find equity: equity = assets - liabilities. To find assets: add liabilities and equity. Example: liabilities 3,000 and equity 5,000 means assets are 8,000. Check by adding back: if equity = assets - liabilities, then liabilities + equity must equal the assets you started with.

questions.section_skill: Explain how deductions and credits differ
questions.outcome_title: Tell a tax deduction from a tax credit, and explain that a deduction does not make a purchase free
questions.intro: Two tax words are often confused. A DEDUCTION lowers the income that tax is calculated on (taxable income). A CREDIT lowers the tax itself, dollar for dollar. Example with a made-up 20 percent rate: a 1,000-dollar deduction lowers taxable income by 1,000 and saves about 0.20 x 1,000 = 200 dollars of tax; a 1,000-dollar credit cuts the tax by 1,000 dollars. Business expenses that are ordinary and necessary for the business are commonly deductible; which credits apply depends on current law, so check with a tax professional.

questions.intro: PAYMENT TERMS say when and how the customer will pay. questions.section_skill: Recognize payment scams and verify before paying
questions.outcome_title: Spot fraud signals in invoices, overpayments and changed payment details
questions.intro: Small businesses are common targets for payment scams. FAKE INVOICES bill for things you never ordered, such as directory listings. CHANGED BANK DETAILS scams send an email that looks like a real supplier asking you to pay a new account. OVERPAYMENT scams send too much money (often by a check that later bounces) and ask you to send back the difference. Protection: match invoices to orders, confirm any bank-detail change by calling a known number (not one in the email), and wait for funds to clear before refunding.

questions.intro: Small businesses are common targets for payment scams. FAKE INVOICES bill for things you never ordered, such as directory listings. CHANGED BANK DETAILS scams send an email that looks like a real supplier asking you to pay a new account. OVERPAYMENT scams send too much money (often by a check that later bounces) and ask you to send back the difference. Protection: match invoices to orders, confirm any bank-detail change by calling a known number (not one in the email), and wait for funds to clear before refunding.
questions.prompt: After a scam, what else should the owner do?

choices.text: Stop using email entirely for the business
Report it and tighten payment checks

questions.correct_answer: Report it and tighten payment checks

wrong_choices.text: Stop using email entirely for the business

questions.section_skill: Plan around supplier terms and communicate delays early
questions.outcome_title: Read supplier terms and tell customers about delays early and honestly
questions.intro: Suppliers have terms too: minimum order quantities, lead time (how long from order to delivery), payment terms, and return rules. Plan orders so supplies arrive before you need them. When something will be late, from your supplier or from you, COMMUNICATE EARLY: tell the customer what happened, the new expected date, and what you will do (for example, offer a choice to wait or cancel). Silence makes customers assume the worst; honest updates keep trust.
questions.prompt: What is lead time?

The time a customer spends reading an ad
The length of a business meeting

questions.correct_answer: How long from order to delivery
questions.feedback: Lead time is the delivery wait.

wrong_choices.text: The time until a loan is repaid
